title: XML and Friends: Parsing, XPath, SVG, RSS and plists
sub: Read, query, build, validate and transform XML in the browser and in Terminal, and know when XML is the right format
goals: Write well-formed XML with declarations, attributes, escaping, CDATA, comments and namespaces
Parse XML in the browser with DOMParser, detect parser errors and serialise documents back to text
Query documents with XPath 1.0 in the browser, in DevTools with $x() and in Terminal with xmllint
Fetch and render an RSS feed and a device inventory, and build XML safely with DOM methods
Draw a live status chart with SVG elements created by createElementNS
Inspect, convert and query macOS property lists, and explain XXE and entity-expansion attacks

blocks.text: XML is the format that quietly runs a large part of your Mac and the web: every `launchd` job, app preference and `Info.plist`, every RSS and Atom feed, every SVG icon, every `.docx` and `.xlsx` file, every sitemap, every Maven `pom.xml` and Android layout. In this chapter you will use the DOM skills from [the previous chapter](#dom) on XML documents: parse the practice server's `/data/devices.xml` and `/data/feed.rss`, query them with XPath, build new XML without opening an injection hole, transform it with XSLT, draw a device-status chart in SVG, and then move to Terminal to validate files with `xmllint` and read and convert property lists with `plutil`. You will also break a document on purpose with one unescaped `&`, which is how most people meet XML's strictness for the first time.
What XML is, and what it is not

**XML** (Extensible Markup Language) is a W3C syntax, first published in 1998 and current as XML 1.0 Fifth Edition (2008), for writing a **tree of named elements** as text. It has no built-in tags. A *vocabulary* defines them: RSS says `<item>` and `<pubDate>`, SVG says `<rect>` and `<circle>`, Apple's plist format says `<dict>` and `<key>`. XML itself only fixes the grammar: how tags, attributes, text and comments are written and how they nest.

The defining property is **strictness**. The XML specification requires a parser to stop at the first *well-formedness* error and report it ("draconian" error handling). HTML went the other way: the HTML standard tells the parser exactly how to repair any input, so a browser never refuses a page. Feed the same broken markup to both parsers:

The message above is Chrome's and Safari's wording (both use libxml2-derived parsers); Firefox reports the same error as `XML Parsing Error: mismatched tag`.

XML is not a database, not a programming language and not a data type system: everything in it is text until a schema or your code says otherwise. It is also not HTML. XHTML is HTML written under XML rules, but browsers only apply those rules when the server sends `Content-Type: application/xhtml+xml`; served as `text/html`, the same file goes through the forgiving HTML parser (see [HTML](#html)).

blocks.text: A document is **well-formed** when it follows the grammar. The rules that catch people:

items.text: Exactly **one root element** wraps everything.
Every start tag has a matching end tag, or is self-closed: `<backup/>`.
Elements **nest properly**: ``, never ``.
Names are **case-sensitive**: `<Name>...</name>` is an error.

Attribute values are **always quoted** (single or double quotes), an attribute appears at most once per element, and HTML's bare attributes are illegal: `<input disabled>` must be `disabled="disabled"`.
`<` and `&` never appear raw in text or attribute values.

Names start with a letter or `_` and may contain letters, digits, `-`, `.` and `_`. Names beginning with `xml` in any case are reserved. A `:` is legal but means a namespace prefix (see [Namespaces](#namespaces)).
The XML declaration, if present, is the very first thing in the file: not even a blank line or a space may come before it.
Comments cannot contain `--`, and cannot appear inside a tag.

blocks.text: Escaping: five entities and character references

XML predefines exactly five **entity references**. Anything else, including HTML favourites like ` ` and `©`, is an error unless a DTD declares it. For any other character, use a numeric **character reference** with the Unicode code point in decimal or hex.

blocks.text: A **CDATA section** (`<![CDATA[ ... ]]>`) holds text that the parser does not scan for markup, so `<` and `&` inside it need no escaping; the only thing it cannot contain is `]]>`. It is handy for embedded code or HTML snippets and changes nothing about the data: to a program, CDATA is just text. **Processing instructions** (`<?target data?>`) carry instructions for a specific application, like `xml-stylesheet` for a browser or an XSLT engine. The XML declaration looks like one but is not a node in the tree.

blocks.text: The document node has three children: the processing instruction (`nodeType` 7), the comment (8) and the root element (1). The declaration is gone: it told the parser the version and encoding and was consumed. The CDATA section is a node of type 4, and its `textContent` is plain text.
Elements or attributes?

Both can hold a value, and vocabularies differ. A rule of thumb that ages well: **attributes for metadata about an element** (identifiers, types, units, flags: `id="1"`, `proto="tcp"`), **elements for content** and for anything that can repeat, has structure of its own, or might need markup inside it (`<port>` appears several times; a `<description>` might contain `<b>`). Attributes cannot repeat, cannot nest and have no order.
Whitespace

Unlike HTML rendering, XML keeps whitespace: the newlines and indentation between tags are text nodes in the tree, exactly as you saw in [the DOM chapter](#dom/tree). Pretty-printing a document (`xmllint --format`) therefore changes it, slightly. Programs that read data-style XML usually ignore whitespace-only text; document-style XML (DocBook, XHTML) can declare `xml:space="preserve"` where it matters.
Namespaces

Vocabularies collide. `<title>` means a page title in XHTML, a tooltip in SVG, and a feed or entry title in Atom. As soon as one document mixes vocabularies (SVG inside XHTML, extension elements inside an Atom feed), a name alone is ambiguous. **XML Namespaces** fix this by pairing every element name with a namespace **URI**.

items.text: `xmlns="URI"` declares the **default namespace** for that element and its descendants: unprefixed element names belong to it.
`xmlns:lab="URI"` binds the **prefix** `lab` to a URI; `<lab:severity>` is then the element `severity` in that namespace.

The URI is an identifier, compared as a string. Nothing fetches it, and it does not have to resolve to a web page. Prefixes are local nicknames: `<a:entry xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">` and `<entry xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">` are the same element.
**Unprefixed attributes are in no namespace**, even inside a default namespace. Only prefixed attributes such as `xlink:href` or `xml:lang` belong to one.

blocks.text: Well-known URIs: XHTML `http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml`, SVG `http://www.w3.org/2000/svg`, XLink `http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink`, Atom `http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom`, XSLT `http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform`, XML Schema `http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema`.

The line that prints `0` is the most common XPath bug in existence. In XPath 1.0 an unprefixed name in an expression means "no namespace", so `//entry` does not match Atom's `entry`, which lives in the Atom namespace. Bind a prefix with a **namespace resolver** function (third argument of `document.evaluate`) and write `//a:entry`, or match on `local-name()` when you do not care. CSS selectors in `querySelector` are more relaxed: a type selector without a namespace matches elements in any namespace, which is why `entry title` found the entry's title.
Well-formed versus valid: DTD and XML Schema

**Well-formed** means the syntax is right. **Valid** means the document also follows a **schema**: which elements may appear, in what order, with which attributes, holding which kinds of values. Browsers only check well-formedness; validation is a separate step you run with a tool.

items.text: A **DTD** (Document Type Definition) is the original schema language, inherited from SGML. It is referenced from a `<!DOCTYPE>` line and can also declare entities. Every Apple plist starts with `<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">`. DTDs know nothing about data types or namespaces.

**XML Schema** (XSD, a W3C Recommendation, versions 1.0 and 1.1) is itself written in XML and has data types (`xs:unsignedShort`, `xs:boolean`, patterns, enumerations). SOAP, Office Open XML and most enterprise formats use it.
**RELAX NG** is a simpler, more readable alternative; **Schematron** adds rule-based checks ("a server must have at least one port").

blocks.text: Here is an XSD for the practice server's device inventory. It says a network holds one or more devices, each with a name, an IPv4-looking address and any number of ports; a port is a number from 0 to 65535 with a `proto` of `tcp` or `udp`.

blocks.text: `broken.xml` is perfectly **well-formed** (any XML parser reads it) and still **invalid**. That is the whole difference. Each error names the file, line, element and the schema rule (a *facet*) that failed, and the exit status is non-zero, so the check slots into scripts and CI with `&&`. Messages and exit codes come from the libxml2 version on your Mac; run `xmllint --version` to see it.

blocks.name: xmllint
blocks.sum: Check, pretty-print, validate and query XML (and parse HTML) from the command line.

how.text: `xmllint` is the command-line front end to **libxml2**, the C library behind much of the XML handling on macOS and Linux. With no options it parses the file and prints it back, so its first use is as a well-formedness checker: any error is printed with the line, a caret under the column, and a non-zero exit status. `-` reads standard input, which makes it a pipeline stage.

`--format` re-indents the output, `--noout` suppresses it (you only want errors), `--schema` validates against an XSD, `--dtdvalid` against an external DTD and `--valid` against the DTD the document declares. `--html` switches to libxml2's HTML parser, which predates HTML5 and complains about tags like `<main>` on stderr; it still builds a tree you can query.

blocks.text: For a new web API, JSON wins: it maps straight onto JavaScript and Python data, it is smaller, and `res.json()` is one call. XML still wins, or is simply what you must speak, in these places:

items.text: **Documents with mixed content**, where markup sits inside running text: DocBook, DITA, XHTML, TEI, legal and publishing formats, and the office formats (`.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx` are zip files of XML; LibreOffice's ODF too).
**Established standards**: RSS and Atom feeds, SVG graphics, `sitemap.xml` for search engines, GPX tracks and KML maps, SAML single sign-on, XMPP chat, SOAP and WSDL services, MusicXML.
**Configuration ecosystems**: Apple property lists, Android layouts and manifests, Maven `pom.xml`, .NET `.csproj`, many Java application servers.
**When validation and transformation tooling matters**: a schema that rejects bad data at the door, and XSLT or XQuery pipelines that publishers have run for decades.

Parsing XML in the browser

`DOMParser` turns a string into a document. With the MIME type `application/xml` (or `text/xml`, `image/svg+xml`, `application/xhtml+xml`) it runs the XML parser and returns an `XMLDocument`; with `text/html` it runs the HTML parser. It never throws on bad input. Instead, the result contains a `<parsererror>` element, whose position and wording differ between engines (Chrome puts it inside the partial document, Firefox makes it the root), so the portable test is "is there a `parsererror` element anywhere?".

Everything from [the DOM chapter](#dom) works on the result, with three differences: matching is **case-sensitive** (`<Device>` is not `<device>`), there is no HTML-only API (`innerText`, `dataset` and the form properties belong to `HTMLElement`; XML elements are plain `Element`s), and the tree keeps every whitespace text node.

`querySelector('Device')` found nothing: XML is case-sensitive. `XMLSerializer` turned the modified element back into text, keeping the original indentation whitespace inside it. Use `serializeToString(doc)` for a whole document; it does not add an XML declaration, so prepend one yourself when the consumer needs it.

blocks.name: DOMParser.parseFromString()
blocks.sum: Parse a string of XML, SVG or HTML into a new Document object.

how.text: The MIME type picks the parser. The XML types run a namespace-aware XML parser and return an `XMLDocument`; `text/html` runs the HTML parser (scripts inside are marked not to run). The new document is not attached to the page and has no rendering, so parsing is safe for display purposes, and you query it with the usual DOM methods.

The XML parser never throws. On a well-formedness error it returns a document containing a `<parsererror>` element with an engine-specific message, and in Chrome a partial tree up to the error. Always test for it before trusting the result.

blocks.name: XMLSerializer.serializeToString()
blocks.sum: Turn a DOM node or document back into XML text, with correct escaping.

how.text: Walks the subtree and writes XML: `&`, `<` and `>` in text become entity references, quotes in attribute values become `"`, empty elements are written self-closed (`<backup/>`), and namespace declarations are added where needed so the output parses back to the same tree. It does not emit an XML declaration and does not pretty-print; whitespace text nodes are written exactly as they are.
Serializing an HTML element gives XHTML-style output with the XHTML namespace on the top element, which is how you produce XML from an HTML page (for example an inline `<svg>` saved as a file).

blocks.text: XPath in depth

CSS selectors can find elements by name, class, attribute and position, and since `:has()` even by their descendants. **XPath** 1.0 (W3C, 1999) goes further: it navigates in every direction (parents, ancestors, preceding siblings), selects attributes and text nodes as results, filters on text content, and computes numbers, strings and booleans. Browsers implement XPath 1.0 only (2.0 and 3.1 exist in tools such as Saxon). It works on HTML pages too, which is why DevTools has `$x()`.

An XPath expression is usually a **location path**: steps separated by `/`, each step written `axis::node-test[predicate]`. A path starting with `/` begins at the document root; otherwise it starts at the **context node** you pass in.

blocks.text: Fetch and render: an RSS feed

**RSS 2.0** is a small vocabulary from the early 2000s: an `<rss>` root, one `<channel>` with a `title`, `link` and `description`, and one `<item>` per entry with `title`, `link`, `description`, `pubDate`, `guid` and `category`. Dates use the old e-mail format of RFC 822 (`Mon, 05 Oct 2026 09:12:00 GMT`), which JavaScript's `Date` parses. **Atom** (RFC 4287) is the stricter successor: namespaced, with `<feed>`, `<entry>` and RFC 3339 dates (`2026-10-05T09:12:00Z`). Feed readers handle both; your router, CI server and home-automation box often publish one.
The practice server's `/data/feed.rss` holds two lab events. Fetch, parse, render with `textContent`:

blocks.page: Lab Status
blocks.out:
Lab Status | application/rss+xml
[
  '2026-10-05 [alert] nas went offline',
  '2026-10-04 [info] pi updated to 6.12'
]

blocks.text: Two habits in that code matter beyond RSS. Dates are printed with `toISOString()`, so the output is the same in every time zone (use `toLocaleString()` with explicit options when you display dates to people). And every piece of feed text goes in through `textContent` and `append`: a feed is **untrusted input**. RSS `<description>` elements routinely carry escaped HTML, and rendering that with `innerHTML` turns anyone who can publish to the feed into someone who can run script on your page ([XSS](#dom/xss)).
Building XML safely

Generating XML with template strings works until a value contains a special character, and then it fails in one of two ways. Either the output is no longer well-formed, or, worse, it is well-formed and **means something else**: an XML injection.

The second document parsed without complaint and now contains an `<admin>true</admin>` element the program never meant to write. If a server trusts that file, a device name just granted admin rights. The fix is the same as for HTML: let a library do the escaping. Build the tree with DOM methods and serialize it; text and attribute values are escaped automatically, so no input can change the structure:

blocks.out:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<network name="R&D "lab""><device id="3" online="true"><name>pi</name><ip>192.168.1.50</ip></device><device id="6" online="true"><name>homeassistant</name><ip>192.168.1.90</ip></device><device><name>cam</name><admin>true</admin></name></device></network>
3 0 cam</name><admin>true</admin>

blocks.text: The hostile name round-trips as data: no `<admin>` element exists, and reading it back gives the exact original string. Where no DOM is available (a Node script, a shell generator), escape every value, replacing `&` **first**:
In Python, `xml.etree.ElementTree` does the same job ([Python's version](#xml/mac) is below), and in Node the capstone builds its XML export with exactly this escaping function.

Text you assign with `textContent` and values you pass to `setAttribute` are stored as data, so the serializer escapes them and no value can inject markup.
`doc.createComment()`, `createCDATASection()` and `createProcessingInstruction()` add the other node types when a format needs them.

blocks.text: XSLT in one example

**XSLT** 1.0 (XSL Transformations, W3C 1999) is a language, written in XML, for transforming XML into XML, HTML or text. A stylesheet is a set of **templates**; each `match`es nodes with an XPath pattern and says what to output for them. The processor walks the input tree and applies the best-matching template to each node. Publishers still run large XSLT pipelines, and it is how a raw RSS or sitemap file can look like a styled page when opened directly in a browser (through an `<?xml-stylesheet?>` instruction).

Chrome deprecated it in 2025; per Chrome's "Removing XSLT" page, XSLT stops working in Chrome 158 (Stable on 17 November 2026) for everyone except sites in an origin trial or browsers under an enterprise policy, and those escape hatches end with Chrome 176 (August 2027). Firefox and WebKit have signalled support for removing it as well. Run XSLT on a server or with `xsltproc` instead, or rewrite small transforms as JavaScript DOM code.

blocks.text: SVG: XML you can script

**SVG** (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML vocabulary for 2-D drawings, rendered natively by every browser. Inside an HTML page you can write `<svg>` inline, and the HTML parser puts it and its children in the SVG namespace automatically. The `viewBox="0 0 360 150"` attribute defines the drawing's own coordinate system (x to the right, y **down**), which the browser scales to whatever size the element gets, so charts stay sharp at any zoom.
From JavaScript, SVG elements must be created **in the SVG namespace**:

Styling properties (`fill`, `stroke`, `opacity`) can come from CSS classes, and CSS wins over the presentation attributes of the same name.

blocks.text: XML on your Mac

macOS stores settings, app metadata and service definitions as **property lists** (plists): `~/Library/Preferences/*.plist`, every app's `Contents/Info.plist`, every `launchd` job in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`. A plist is a tree of `<dict>` (alternating `<key>` and value), `<array>`, `<string>`, `<integer>`, `<real>`, `<true/>`, `<false/>`, `<date>` and `<data>` (base64). It can be stored in three encodings that hold the same tree: **XML** (readable), **binary** (`bplist00` magic bytes; what most of the system writes) and, for conversion, **JSON**. [System, Processes & macOS Tools](#system/settings) covers `defaults`, which edits preferences through the plist APIs; here you work on the files.
Create a `launchd` agent definition (the kind you would write to run `netcheck.zsh` every five minutes) in `~/lab/xml`:

<plist version="1.0">

blocks.text: The `plutil` lines are exact for macOS 15 and later: Apple publishes that `plutil` as open source in the `swift-corelibs-foundation` project, and its code fixes the formats shown (`path: OK` for `-lint`; `-p` with `=>`, two-space indents, keys sorted case-insensitively; one value plus a newline for `-extract ... raw`). The `xmllint` lines match the libxml2 2.9.13 that macOS ships (Apple's `libxml2-39` source). Without `2>&1 | head -1`, xmllint also prints the offending line, which here is binary noise, and a `^` under the error position.

The XPath pattern `//key[.='X']/following-sibling::*[1]` is the standard way to read a plist with generic XML tools: plists pair each `<key>` with the **next sibling** element, so "the value of key X" is "the first element after the key whose text is X". `plutil -p` reads binary and XML alike and is meant for humans (its format is not stable for scripts); `plutil -extract key raw` is the script-friendly way to read one value.

`plutil -convert xml1 file.plist` replaces the file with the converted version. Add `-o -` to print to stdout or `-o copy.plist` to write elsewhere, and work on copies of anything under `~/Library` or `/Library`: `cp ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dock.plist /tmp/dock.plist` first. JSON has no date or binary-data type, so `plutil -convert json` refuses plists that contain `<date>` or `<data>` values.

blocks.name: xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring()
blocks.sum: Parse XML text into an Element tree you can iterate, search with a small XPath subset, modify and serialize.
blocks.syntax: ET.fromstring(text) -> Element    ET.parse(path).getroot()    el.find(path) / findall(path) / findtext(path)    el.get(attr)    ET.tostring(el, encoding='unicode')

how.text: `fromstring` parses a string, `parse` a file. An `Element` has `tag`, `attrib` (a dict), `text` and its children, and it is iterable. `iter('name')` walks all descendants with that tag; `find`, `findall` and `findtext` accept a subset of XPath (`.//device[@online='true']/name`, positions, attribute tests, but no functions like `count()`). `SubElement` builds new nodes and `tostring` serializes with escaping, just like the DOM in the browser.
It uses the Expat parser, which does not fetch external entities. For untrusted input the separate `defusedxml` package rejects entity declarations entirely. For plists use `plistlib` instead.

examples.desc: Names of online devices
examples.code:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
root = ET.fromstring("<n><d on='1'><name>pi</name></d><d on='0'><name>nas</name></d></n>")
print([e.text for e in root.findall(".//d[@on='1']/name")])

blocks.text: XML security: XXE and entity expansion
The DTD part of XML can declare **entities**, named replacements that the parser expands. That one feature causes two classic attacks on software that parses XML from someone else.

**XXE (XML External Entity).** An *external* entity's value is a URI, and a parser that resolves it reads that file or URL and pastes the contents into the document. If a server parses uploaded XML that way and echoes any part of it back, an attacker can read files on the server (`file:///etc/passwd`, configuration with database passwords) or make the server request internal URLs (server-side request forgery). Try it safely on your own Mac with a file of your own:

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab/xml
echo 'wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery' > secret.txt
cat > xxe.xml <<'XML'
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE note [
  <!ENTITY leak SYSTEM "secret.txt">
]>
<note>&leak;</note>
XML

$ xmllint --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml

$ xmllint --noent --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml
wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery

$ xmllint --noent --nonet --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml
wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery

blocks.text: By default libxml2 leaves the entity unexpanded and the note is empty. `--noent` ("substitute entities") makes it read the file, which is the server-side mistake in miniature. `--nonet` only blocks *network* fetches; local files still leak.
**Billion laughs (entity expansion).** Internal entities can refer to each other. Ten references to an entity that holds ten references, nine levels deep, expand three bytes into about 3 GB:

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
  <!ENTITY lol "lol">
  <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
  <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
  <!-- ... up to lol9: each level multiplies the size by 10 -->
]>
<lolz>&lol3;</lolz>

blocks.text: With three levels as shown it is a harmless 300 characters. Current libxml2 stops the full version with `Maximum entity amplification factor exceeded` and `Detected an entity reference loop`, and Python's bundled Expat has similar limits in recent releases, but older parsers simply run out of memory. Do not test the nine-level version on software you are unsure about.

blocks.title: Rules for parsing XML you did not write

items.text: Browsers are on the safe side: `DOMParser` never loads external entities and caps expansion. The risk is on **servers** and in tools: an upload endpoint, a SOAP service, a SAML login, an office-file importer, a feed fetcher.

Turn off DTD processing and external entities in whatever library you use (OWASP's *XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet* lists the settings for Java, .NET, PHP, Python and others). Never pass `--noent` to `xmllint` or `resolve_entities=True` to `lxml` for untrusted input.

In Python, the standard library's Expat does not fetch external entities, but check `pyexpat.EXPAT_VERSION` (the docs ask for 2.7.2 or later for full expansion protection) and use the `defusedxml` package, which refuses DTD entity declarations outright.
Validate the shape (a schema, or the root-element check you saw above) and escape on output: XML injection is the same class of bug as XSS and SQL injection.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **An unescaped `&` or `<`** in text or an attribute: `EntityRef: expecting ';'` or `StartTag: invalid element name`. Write `&` and `<`, or build with DOM methods.
**HTML entities in XML**: ` ` and `©` are undefined. Use ` ` and `©`.
**Anything before the XML declaration**: a blank line, a space, or a debugging `echo` in a script that generates XML. The declaration must come first (only a byte order mark may precede it).
**Assuming `DOMParser` throws**: it returns a document with `<parsererror>`. Check for it every time.
**Forgetting the default namespace in XPath**: `//entry` and `//rect` match nothing in Atom and SVG documents. Use a resolver or `local-name()`.
**`//x[1]` when you meant `(//x)[1]`**: the first is "first child of each parent".
**`createElement('rect')` for SVG**: invisible unknown elements. Use `createElementNS`.
**Building XML with template strings**: one quote or ampersand breaks it, and a crafted value injects elements.
**`plutil -convert` without `-o`**: the original file is rewritten.

**Comparing XML as text**: attribute order, quotes, whitespace and `` versus `` differ without changing the data. Parse both sides and compare trees, or normalize with a canonicalizer (`xmllint --c14n`).

task.text: The page holds the device inventory in a `<script type="application/xml" id="data">` element (it is not executed, just stored). Set each variable to an XPath expression; the check evaluates them against that document.

items.text: `q1`: the names of all devices (router, pi, nas)
`q2`: the IP address of the device named nas
`q3`: the **number** of online devices
`q4`: the ports greater than 1024
`q5`: the names of devices that have more than one port

task.text: Try your expressions in the xpath widget above first.

hints: `//device/name` for q1. For q2, put a predicate on the device: `//device[name='nas']/ip`.
`count(...)` returns a number; `[. > 1024]` filters ports by value; `[count(port) > 1]` filters devices.

why.text: Each answer is one step plus one predicate: predicates are where XPath does its filtering. `count()` changes the result type from a node set to a number. In q4, the comparison converts each port's text to a number before comparing, which is why `8080 > 1024` works on text content.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: one ampersand

task.text: Run the starter. It prints a parser error instead of the network name and printer name, because the XML contains raw `&` characters. Fix the **XML text** (not the parsing code) so that it prints exactly `R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser`. Read the error message first: it tells you the line and column.

hints: There are two ampersands, one in an attribute value and one in text. Both need escaping.
The entity for `&` is `&`. The parser turns it back into `&`, so the printed output still shows a plain ampersand.

why.text: `&` starts an entity reference, so a parser that meets `&D lab"` looks for a name followed by `;` and stops when it does not find one. Escaping is a property of the *serialized* text only: after parsing, `getAttribute` and `textContent` return the plain characters. The same file fails `xmllint --noout` with `EntityRef: expecting ';'` and a caret under the column.

blocks.check:
assert(!/NOT WELL-FORMED/.test(out), 'The XML still does not parse: escape every & as &.');
assert(out.trim() === 'R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser', 'Expected exactly "R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser"; got ' + JSON.stringify(out.trim()));

blocks.title: A plist, converted and queried in Terminal

task.text: In `~/lab/xml`, create `netcheck.plist` as shown in [XML on your Mac](#xml/mac), convert it to **binary**, and confirm with `file` that it is binary. Then, without converting the file back, print only the value of `StartInterval` (300) using `plutil` to produce XML on stdout and `xmllint --xpath` to select the value. Finally print the second program argument with `plutil -extract`.

hints: `plutil -convert xml1 -o - netcheck.plist` writes XML to stdout without touching the file. `xmllint` reads stdin when the file name is `-`.
In a plist the value is the element right after its `<key>`: `//key[.='StartInterval']/following-sibling::*[1]/text()`. Key paths for `-extract` use dots and zero-based indexes: `ProgramArguments.1`.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab/xml
plutil -convert binary1 netcheck.plist
file netcheck.plist
plutil -convert xml1 -o - netcheck.plist | xmllint --xpath "//key[.='StartInterval']/following-sibling::*[1]/text()" -
plutil -extract ProgramArguments.1 raw netcheck.plist

why.text: `-o -` turns `plutil` into a converter stage, so binary plists (the format most of macOS writes) become readable by any XML tool without modifying them. The `following-sibling::*[1]` idiom exists because plists pair keys and values by position, not by nesting.

blocks.title: An SVG bar chart from /api/devices

task.text: Fetch `/api/devices`, count the devices of each `type`, and sort the types alphabetically. For the type at index `i` draw a `rect` in `#chart` with `x = i * 50 + 10`, `width = 40`, `height = count * 40` and `y = 120 - height`, plus a `text` label with the type name at `x = i * 50 + 30`, `y = 135`. Print one line per type: `type count`. Create every SVG element with `createElementNS`.

hints: Count with `const counts = {}; for (const d of devices) counts[d.type] = (counts[d.type] ?? 0) + 1;` and sort with `Object.keys(counts).sort()`.
For each attribute call `rect.setAttribute('height', h)`. Use `text.setAttribute('text-anchor', 'middle')` to centre the labels.

why.text: SVG's y axis points down, so a bar of height `h` standing on the line y = 120 starts at `120 - h`. The small `el()` factory hides the namespace and attribute boilerplate; it is the same helper the status-chart playground uses, and the seed of every hand-written chart library.

blocks.title: XML, JSON or HTML?

task.text: For each job, pick a format and give one reason: (a) the response of your own new `/api/devices` endpoint consumed by your dashboard's JavaScript; (b) a feed of lab alerts that any feed reader on your phone should be able to subscribe to; (c) a launchd job that runs a script every five minutes; (d) an icon for the dashboard that must look sharp on a Retina display and change colour with the theme; (e) a report a colleague will open and edit in Word.

blocks.solution:
(a) JSON: native to JavaScript (res.json()), compact, typed numbers and booleans.
(b) XML: RSS 2.0 or Atom, because feed readers speak those standards.
(c) XML (plist): launchd reads property lists; write XML, plutil -lint it, macOS may store it as binary.
(d) XML (SVG): vector, scriptable, styleable with CSS classes and currentColor.
(e) XML inside a zip (.docx, Office Open XML): generate it with a library rather than by hand.

why.text: The choice is mostly made by the **consumer**. Where a standard or an existing tool reads the data, speak its format; where you control both ends and the data is records, JSON is simpler. XML wins when the content is a document, when a vocabulary already exists, or when validation and transformation tooling is part of the job.

questions.q: Which of these is well-formed XML?

options.text: `<device id=3><name>pi</name></device>`
`<device id="3"><Name>pi</name></device>`
`<device id="3"><name>R&D pi</name><backup/></device>`
`<device id="3"><name>pi</device></name>`

questions.why: Attribute values must be quoted, names are case-sensitive, elements must nest properly, and `&` must be written `&`. Only the third follows every rule.

questions.q: An XML file contains ` ` and no DTD. What happens when you parse it?

options.text: It becomes a no-break space, as in HTML
It is kept as the literal text " "
The parser reports an undefined entity error
It becomes an ordinary space

questions.why: XML predefines only `< > & " '`. Write a no-break space as ` `.

questions.q: Which XPath expression returns only the first port element in the whole document?

options.text: `//port[last()]`
`/port[1]`

questions.why: `//port[1]` selects every port that is the first port child of its parent (one per device). The parentheses build the full set first, then take its first member.

questions.q: A feed starts with `<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">`. Why does `//entry` select nothing?

options.text: Atom feeds cannot be queried with XPath
Unprefixed names in XPath 1.0 mean "no namespace", but entry is in the Atom namespace
The expression needs a trailing /text()
Browsers only support XPath on HTML documents

questions.why: Bind a prefix through a namespace resolver (`//a:entry`) or match `//*[local-name()='entry']`.

questions.q: Your script calls `document.createElement('circle')`, sets `cx`, `cy` and `r`, and appends it to an `<svg>`. Nothing is drawn. What fixes it?
questions.why: `createElement` makes an HTML element named circle. SVG shapes must be created in the SVG namespace with `document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'circle')`.

terms.def: Extensible Markup Language: a strict text syntax for trees of named elements, with vocabularies defined on top
Following XML's grammar: one root, closed and nested tags, quoted attributes, escaped & and <
Well-formed and also conforming to a schema (DTD, XML Schema or RELAX NG)
Document Type Definition: the original XML schema language, also able to declare entities
XSD, a W3C schema language written in XML, with data types and patterns
A URI that qualifies element and attribute names so vocabularies can be mixed without collisions
A named escape such as & or < that the parser replaces with characters
A <![CDATA[ ... ]]> block whose text is not scanned for markup
A language for selecting nodes and computing values in an XML or HTML tree; browsers support version 1.0
A template language, written in XML, for transforming XML into XML, HTML or text
Scalable Vector Graphics: an XML vocabulary for 2-D drawings rendered natively by browsers
Apple's plist format for settings and metadata, stored as XML, binary or JSON
XML External Entity attack: a parser that resolves external entities leaks files or makes requests
An entity-expansion attack where nested entities blow a tiny document up to gigabytes
